n: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
w: Te Papa means 'the treasure box' in Maori, and the name is a mission statement: a museum built on the idea that taonga carry living stories, not just labels. Born from a 1998 merger of the old National Museum and National Art Gallery, it now pulls over a million visitors a year off the Wellington waterfront.
s: NZ's national museum, built on living stories
_facts: New Zealand's national museum, opened 1998 after merging the National Museum of NZ and National Art Gallery
average of more than 1.1 million visitors a year, 58th-most-visited art gallery in the world in 2023
operates under a bicultural philosophy emphasising the living stories behind its cultural treasures

w: An island that has done a bit of everything: refuge for early Maori, quarantine station for sick arrivals off ships, internment camp for 'enemy aliens' in two world wars, gun emplacements against an invasion that never came, then decades as an animal quarantine post. Since 1981 it's been left to heal into native bush.
s: Quarantine island, internment camp, now sanctuary
_facts: largest of three islands in Wellington Harbour; used as refuge by pre-colonial Maori, middens found
human quarantine station 1840s-1920s; 'enemy aliens' interned there in both world wars; WWII anti-aircraft emplacements remain
animal quarantine 1864-1995; restoration to native forest began 1981, now home to native birds, reptiles and plants

w: Four buildings, four eras of taste, one site: an 1899 library, an Edwardian Parliament House, the deliberately round 'Beehive' from 1977, and a 1991 office tower. Historians have politely called the ensemble incoherent - maybe the most honest description of a working democracy's headquarters anywhere.
s: Four eras of architecture, one seat of government
_facts: 45,000 sqm site at the northern end of Lambton Quay, Wellington
comprises the Parliamentary Library (1899), Edwardian neoclassical Parliament House (1922), the executive wing 'The Beehive' (1977), and Bowen House (1991)
overall setting described as having 'little aesthetic or architectural coherence'

w: Matairangi to Maori, 'Mt Vic' to everyone else - a 196-metre hill that somehow squeezes a full 360-degree view of Wellington into one lookout: the harbour, Evans Bay, the Miramar Peninsula, and the whole city spilling down toward the water. A short climb for one of the best payoffs in town.
s: A short climb, a 360-degree view of Wellington
_facts: 196-metre hill immediately east of central Wellington, known as Matairangi, colloquially Mt Vic
borders the suburbs of Oriental Bay, Roseneath, Hataitai and Newtown
summit lookout gives 360-degree views over the city, suburbs, harbour, Evans Bay and the Miramar Peninsula

w: Wellingtonians still call it 'the Basilica' for its Palladian lines, though it only earned the title of cathedral in 1984, after earthquake strengthening finally caught up with a parish that had been serving Thorndon since 1850 - decades before there was even an archdiocese to need a seat.
s: The 'Basilica' that became a cathedral in 1984
_facts: Roman Catholic cathedral on Hill Street, Wellington, seat of the Archbishop of Wellington
parish church of the Thorndon Catholic parish, founded 1850, predating the cathedral designation
popularly known as 'the Basilica' for its Palladian style; designated cathedral in 1984 after earthquake strengthening

w: Behind a predator-proof fence in the hills above Karori, 225 hectares of old water-catchment forest is being coaxed back to what it looked like before rats and stoats arrived. Call it the world's first mainland island: fence out every introduced pest, and native tui and kaka start turning up in the suburbs again.
s: A fenced-off forest bringing birds back to the city
_facts: formerly Karori Wildlife Sanctuary, first urban completely fenced ecosanctuary, restoring biodiversity across 225ha of forest
previously part of Wellington's water catchment area, surrounded by a pest-exclusion fence
credited with the increased sightings of native tui and kaka in Wellington's suburbs; described as the world's first mainland island sanctuary in an urban environment

w: Built in 1924 at the foot of Mount Victoria, the Embassy is the last purpose-built 1920s cinema in the country still screening films rather than sitting as a heritage curiosity. Ownership has passed council to trust to multiplex chain over the decades, but the picture-palace bones still do the job.
_facts: cinema built 1924, at the eastern end of Courtenay Place in the shadow of Mount Victoria
owned by Wellington City Council, management rights sold to SKYCITY Cinemas 2005, now part of Event Cinemas
recognised as a place of historical and cultural significance by Heritage NZ, the only custom-built 1920s cinema still in use in New Zealand

w: Until 1998, this was the second-largest wooden building on the planet, beaten only by a Buddhist temple in Nara - an odd distinction for the office block that once ran the young colonial government from reclaimed harbour mud. Victoria University's law students now study inside an architectural record-holder.
s: The world's second-largest wooden building, till 1998
_facts: completed 1876 on land reclaimed from Wellington Harbour, built to house the young NZ Government and public service
now houses the law school of Victoria University of Wellington; Category 1 historic building
until 1998 was the second-largest wooden building in the world after Todai-ji in Nara, Japan

w: Thirty thousand and eight names are carved into the Rolls of Honour inside the Hall of Memories - every one of New Zealand's war dead since the Boer War. An unknown warrior was finally given a tomb here in 2004, decades after the carillon and hall were first dedicated on Anzac Day, 1932.
_facts: dedicated 1932 on Anzac Day, commemorates NZ war dead from the Boer War, WWI, WWII, Korea, Malaysia and Vietnam
comprises the War Memorial Carillon and Hall of Memories; tomb of an unknown NZ warrior added 2004
Rolls of Honour bear the names of 30,108 of NZ's war dead; Category 1 Historic Place

w: A Victorian bond store on the waterfront hides a Pepper's-ghost theatre for Maori legend, a memorial to the Wahine ferry disaster, and something called the Wellington Time Machine - enough that The Times named it one of the world's fifty best museums in 2013. All inside an 1892 warehouse built to store goods.
s: An 1892 bond store, one of the world's best museums
_facts: occupies the 1892 Bond Store on Jervois Quay, Queens Wharf; voted one of the world's 50 best museums by The Times in 2013
four floors covering Wellington's history: early Maori and European settlement, maritime history, city growth
three theatre areas including a Pepper's-ghost telling of Maori legends and a memorial to the Wahine ferry sinking

w: A decade-long trade dispute held up construction so long that by the time this stark black tower finally topped out in 1984, Wellington got to call it the tallest building in the country - for all of two years, until Auckland took the title back. The square, uncompromising modernism still dominates Willis Street.
s: The tallest tower in NZ, for exactly two years
_facts: completed 1984 as the State Insurance Building, at 1 Willis Street, Wellington
was the tallest building in NZ on completion, overtaking the 87m Quay Tower in Auckland; late International Style modernism
construction delayed a decade by a trade dispute; remained tallest in NZ until 1986 when the BNZ Tower in Auckland opened

w: Suzanne Aubert, the nun revered as one of New Zealand's great humanitarians, was farewelled from this church in 1926 - a fitting send-off for a parish that has run on Marist Fathers and a serious choral tradition since a Capuchin friar named Jeremiah O'Reily founded it in the 1870s.
s: Where Suzanne Aubert's funeral was held, 1926
_facts: Catholic church at the corner of Boulcott Street and O'Reily Avenue, Wellington
Marist Fathers have provided clergy since 1874, succeeding founding priest Fr Jeremiah O'Reily; used as Archbishop O'Shea's pro-cathedral 1936-1954
site of the funeral of Suzanne Aubert in 1926; known for its church music tradition

w: Opened in 1912 as His Majesty's Theatre and designed by a New Zealander who made his name building playhouses, the St James is now where the Royal New Zealand Ballet calls home - a proscenium stage on Courtenay Place old enough to have changed its name more than once and never lost its Category 1 heritage status.
s: The 1912 stage the Royal NZ Ballet calls home
_facts: built as His Majesty's Theatre, designed 1912 by NZ-born theatre designer Henry Eli White
large proscenium stage theatre, home to the Royal New Zealand Ballet, on Courtenay Place
classified as a Category 1 Historic Place by Heritage New Zealand

w: Designed in the 1930s but not finished until 1998, this Anglican cathedral took 64 years from drawing board to consecration - the 1931 Napier quake convinced its architect to pour it entirely in concrete. Built as a war memorial, it replaced Old St Paul's as cathedral in 1964, decades before the building was done.
s: A cathedral 64 years in the making
_facts: Anglican cathedral at Hill Street and Molesworth Street, Thorndon, designed in the 1930s by architect Cecil Wood
construction began 1954, completed 1998, built in reinforced concrete due to lessons from the 1931 Napier earthquake
envisioned as a war memorial cathedral; began use as cathedral 1964 replacing Old St Paul's; consecrated 2001

w: A tiny chapel named for the Pacific island where a missionary was martyred in 1841 - and one of the most celebrated buildings New Zealand architecture has produced, winning a gold medal in 1968 and a 25-year award for holding up in 1986. John Scott built it small and let the design do all the talking.
s: A tiny chapel, twice awarded by NZ architects
_facts: designed by architect John Scott, built by the brothers of the Society of Mary
named after the Pacific island of Futuna where missionary Peter Chanel was martyred in 1841
won the NZ Institute of Architects gold medal in 1968 and its 25-year award in 1986; Category 1 Historic Site

w: Standing dark now at Pencarrow Head, this decommissioned light once guided ships around the tricky approach to Wellington Harbour before its duties were handed off elsewhere - a lonely coastal marker still worth the walk out to see.
s: A decommissioned light at the harbour's mouth
_facts: decommissioned lighthouse at Pencarrow Head in the Wellington region

w: Te Whare Toi, 'the house of art' in Maori, is Wellington's dedicated public gallery for contemporary work - a rotating exhibition programme rather than a permanent collection, keeping the city's civic art space busy with whatever's current.
_facts: public art gallery in Wellington, New Zealand, known as Te Whare Toi

w: NZ's second-ever liquor licence went to this pub in 1840, when the tide lapped close enough that patrons arrived by boat - legend says the Ngati Toa chief Te Rauparaha among them. Fire gutted it in 1866, but the Thistle rebuilt in months, then turned up in a Katherine Mansfield story. Declared NZ's oldest pub, 2008.
s: NZ's oldest pub, said to have ferried in a Maori chief
_facts: one of NZ's oldest public houses, built 1840 by William Couper, received the second liquor licence issued in the country

original timber building destroyed by fire 1866, rebuilt as two storeys within months; pre-1876 reclamation stood a few metres from the shoreline, with patrons said to include the Ngati Toa chief Te Rauparaha
featured in Katherine Mansfield's 1907 short story 'Leves Amores'; declared NZ's oldest pub in 2008
